reason: Gives a test from the attacker's side: what would they have to defeat (software or hardware logic, a rule imposed on people, or a physical obstacle). It sorts all six items: firewall and FDE are logic, door and fence are obstacles, AUP and background check are processes imposed on people. This is a different test from hint 1's 'enforcer, not asset'. Small wobble: 'hardware' sits next to 'physical obstacle', so a learner could ask whether a door lock counts as hardware. The word 'logic' mostly settles that.

Splits the items that look like honesty by asking whose relationship the honest act serves. Telling a client you aren't qualified and refusing a conflict of interest go to III. Reporting the exam-question seller goes to IV. Declining to exaggerate to a prospect (not yet a client) and refusing an unauthorised scan stay in II. This fixes a weak spot in hint 0: the 'would you owe it if nobody hired you' test could push the 'beyond my qualifications' item into II. I checked all eight items and none is steered wrong.

Targets the trap in the prompt: the risk is 'already raised', so a learner may skip identification and start at assessment. 'Raising is not understanding' plus 'what must you write down before you can compare' puts Identify before Assess/rank. Its scope is narrow, since it only orders the first two steps. Minor risk: 'write down' echoes 'Document the residual risk', but 'before you could compare' anchors it to the start.

The method is circular. Each step's evidence first exists when that step is done, so 'order by when the evidence could first exist' is just 'order the steps' with an audit story on top. It gives no test for the pairs a novice actually finds hard: assess vs choose treatment, and apply/verify vs document and accept the residual. Residual acceptance is often signed off when the treatment is chosen, so evidence timing doesn't even separate those last two. The 'audit' picture only confirms what is already obvious, that documentation comes last.

The 'survives replacing every technology' test sorts the two standards wrongly. 'Run the approved hardened OS image' still holds after a full tech refresh, because a new approved image gets defined. 'Encrypt data at rest with AES-256' names an algorithm, not a product, so it also survives replacing hardware and software. Both pass the survival test and get pushed up to Policy. The test does work for procedures (console steps, the Report button) and for the two policy statements. It also doesn't separate Standard from Procedure, since both 'get rewritten'. The test should ask whether the item names a specific technology or setting, not whether that technology will change.
